# eb-stack

> eb-stack parses conda-forge, Spack, PyPI, CRAN, Cargo, LuaRocks, Raku, and EasyBuild recipes into one package plan, a planned CycloneDX SBOM, Resolvo locks, and conventional EasyBuild recipes.

This file is the manual in one document. The short index is llms.txt.

# eb-stack

# What it is

  `eb-stack` parses conda-forge, Spack, and [EasyBuild](https://docs.easybuild.io/) recipes into one
  canonical package plan. It emits a planned CycloneDX Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), materializes
  independently installable profiles, applies distribution/site preferences
  inside [Resolvo](https://github.com/mamba-org/resolvo), writes one lock and conventional `.eb` file per profile,
  and drives the resulting bundle through a persisted target-routed build
  campaign. Existing-recipe bumps use the same manifest, SBOM, solver, and
  campaign artifacts as new packages.

# What it is not

  - **Not** an EasyBuild replacement. `eb-stack` routes `eb --robot` through a
    configured target; EasyBuild still implements all build and install steps.
  - **Not** a general-purpose Python dependency resolver. The domain model is
    EasyBuild's `name` / `version` / `toolchain` / `dependencies` shape only.
  - **Not** a post-install compliance scanner. The emitted SBOM is a **planned**
    inventory. Binary verification is a separate campaign claim.

# Install

  No public release is published. Build from source with Rust 1.88 or newer:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/HaoZeke/eb-stack.git
cd eb-stack
cargo test --locked
cargo build --locked --release
# binary: target/release/eb-stack
install -Dm755 target/release/eb-stack ~/.local/bin/eb-stack
```

  Verify:

```bash
eb-stack --version
```

# Inspect from a fresh clone

  The bundled conda-forge eOn recipe and public profile make the parser and
  artifact boundary runnable without EasyBuild or an external robot tree:

```bash
eb-stack package inspect \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \
  --format conda-forge \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \
  --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/eon-inspect

python3 -m json.tool /tmp/eon-inspect/package.plan.json >/dev/null
python3 -m json.tool /tmp/eon-inspect/package.sbom.cdx.json >/dev/null
```

  The two files are the canonical build manifest and planned CycloneDX SBOM.
  Inspection does not solve dependencies, emit recipes, or establish a build
  claim; those stages need an EasyBuild robot tree and configured target.

# Tutorial: foreign recipe to verified EasyBuild package

This tutorial plans conda-forge eOn, explains the artifacts, and routes the
result into a build campaign. The QMCPACK path differs only in parser and
package configuration.

# Prepare the runnable local target

The public tutorial target runs EasyBuild inside the repository's Rocky Linux
Podman image. Build the image and copy the upstream robot plus the eOn fixture
overlay into the path namespace mounted by the target:

```bash
podman build -t eb-stack-rocky9 \
  -f skills/new-package/container/rocky9/Containerfile \
  skills/new-package/container/rocky9

mkdir -p \
  /tmp/eb-stack/robot \
  /tmp/eb-stack/overlay \
  /tmp/eb-stack/sources \
  /tmp/eb-stack/bundles

scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh
set -a
source "${EB_UPSTREAM_CACHE:-$HOME/.cache/eb-stack/upstream}/env.sh"
set +a
rsync -a "$EB_EASYCONFIGS"/ \
  /tmp/eb-stack/robot/
rsync -a fixtures/eon_core_rgpot/easyconfigs/ \
  /tmp/eb-stack/overlay/
```

Set the paths used throughout the tutorial:

```bash
export ROBOT=/tmp/eb-stack/robot
export BUNDLE=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-tutorial
export STATE=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-tutorial.campaign.json
```

The bundle path is identical on the host and in the container. Probe every
target layer before planning a long build:

```bash
eb-stack target doctor \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9
```

# Inspect the conda-forge recipe

```bash
eb-stack package inspect \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \
  --format conda-forge \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \
  --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/eon-inspect
```

Open `/tmp/eon-inspect/package.plan.json`. Important sections are:

- `origin` and `package`: foreign identity with configured EasyBuild policy;
- `sources`: every source artifact and checksum;
- `dependencies`: roles, constraints, conditions, and provenance;
- `build`: EasyBuild easyblock, toolchain, and configuration;
- `profiles`: independently installable products;
- `outputs`: requested profile/stack pairs;
- `residuals`: dynamic or ambiguous input that needs judgment.

The planned CycloneDX document is emitted at the same boundary. It describes
the requested pre-build inventory and never claims installed evidence.

# Resolve and emit

```bash
eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \
  --format conda-forge \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \
  --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \
  --easyconfigs "$ROBOT" \
  --easyconfigs /tmp/eb-stack/overlay \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/eon-foss-2026.1.toml \
  --out-dir "$BUNDLE"
```

The generated tree contains:

```text
package.plan.json
package.sbom.cdx.json
closure.plan.json
closure.sbom.cdx.json
build-order.json
locks/default.lock.json
easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0-foss-2026.1.eb
easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0_safemath-eigen5-core-guard.patch
```

The lock is the actual Resolvo result. Its direct dependencies name selected
versions, toolchains, versionsuffixes, source easyconfig paths, build/runtime
roles, pin outcomes, and candidate exclusions.

# Understand stack pin fallback

`examples/stacks/eon-foss-2026.1.toml` records the Eigen 5 identity required
by the safemath core-guard patch without imposing it on unrelated package
plans. It is a `preferred` pin with the complete EasyBuild toolchain and
versionsuffix identity. Resolvo admits the pinned artifact's dependency
closure, then first tries that favored candidate. If another declared
requirement or known exclusion makes it infeasible, the solver selects a
compatible alternative and sets `fallback = true` with a reason in the lock.
Change the mode to `locked` only when the stack requires that exact candidate
and must fail otherwise. The core + rgpot product needs no cross-generation
pins; every dependency sits on the foss-2026.1 / GCCcore-15.2.0 generation.

A version range is not build evidence. A candidate can be
SAT-compatible and still fail configure, compile, link, tests, install, or
sanity. Those outcomes belong to the campaign finding model.

# Check the emitted recipe

```bash
RECIPE="$BUNDLE/easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0-foss-2026.1.eb"

eb-stack recipe format "$RECIPE"
eb-stack recipe lint "$RECIPE"
eb-stack recipe check \
  --recipe "$RECIPE" \
  --easyconfigs "$ROBOT" \
  --easyconfigs /tmp/eb-stack/overlay \
  --easyconfigs "$BUNDLE/easyconfigs"
```

At this point the bundle may claim **resolves**. No build has occurred.

# Probe the target

```bash
eb-stack target list \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml

eb-stack target doctor \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9
```

Read all four checks. A healthy transport does not imply a healthy executor,
runtime, or EasyBuild command.

# Run and repair the campaign

```bash
eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle "$BUNDLE" \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9 \
  --state "$STATE"

eb-stack campaign status --state "$STATE"
```

`campaign run` stays in the foreground. Keep that shell under the process
supervisor used by the target site and use another shell for `campaign status`.
If the controlling process is interrupted, first confirm that the routed
container, scheduler job, or host command has stopped, then rerun with the same
state path. The state remains the audit record; do not start a duplicate state
for the same bundle.

If the campaign fails, `campaign status` prints the finding id. Claim that
id and record the repair with the commands in
[Repair a failed campaign](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/howto/repair-campaign.html.md). Run the campaign
again with the same state. Successful stages supersede stale open findings.
`builds` becomes true only after all emitted recipes succeed.
`binary_verified` becomes true only when at least one declared verification
command exists and all such commands succeed.

# Route the same bundle again

The same public target runs a second time against the bundle this tutorial
already planned. `examples/targets/site.example.toml` is the file to copy
when a site fills in its own host, image, and scheduler. This checkout runs
the local target:

```bash
eb-stack target doctor \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9

eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle "$BUNDLE" \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9 \
  --state "$STATE"
```

The bundle must be visible at the same absolute path used by the selected
runtime. The local target mounts `/tmp/eb-stack`, which is why `$BUNDLE`
lives there.

# Try QMCPACK variants

Replace the source and package-config arguments:

```bash
eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/spack_qmcpack/package.py \
  --format spack \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \
  --package-config examples/packages/qmcpack.toml \
  --source-checksum 511d5f368db002f2f77504619e1ada8d4a3034200d25feef6773d12a6ed6d18e \
  --easyconfigs "$ROBOT" \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/qmcpack_foss_2026_1/easyconfigs \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/foss-2026.1.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/qmcpack-tutorial
```

QMCPACK emits one unsuffixed default recipe and one `-complex` recipe because
the latter is an independently loadable product variant. Both profiles get
their own lock and must build in the campaign. The source checksum is explicit
because this Spack package pins the release by Git commit rather than by the
SHA-256 of its GitHub archive.

# Run an annual toolchain-generation bump

The annual workflow applies the canonical bump bundle to each maintained
recipe, then drives every bundle through the same target-routed build campaign.
Dependency version selection is mechanical; build failures remain typed repair
work.

# Prepare the generation inputs

Record:

- the source and target toolchain generations;
- upstream EasyBuild robot roots and site overlays;
- the stack-policy TOML file for site/distribution preferences;
- the public target base plus the site target layer;
- the maintained recipe list and destination easyconfigs repository.

The site layer owns hostnames, scheduler sizing, module setup, durable build
paths, container images, and environment. Do not put those values in the
public skill.

# Generate one canonical bundle per recipe

```bash
eb-stack package bump \
  --source tests/repro_fixtures/gromacs/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2023b.eb \
  --toolchain foss/2024a \
  --easyconfigs tests/repro_fixtures/universe_foss_2024a \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a
```

Repeat mechanically for the maintained set. Each successful bundle contains a
manifest, planned Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), default profile lock, and recipe. The lock records stack
pin fallbacks and exclusions, making generation policy reviewable.

Explicit dependency toolchain families are retargeted with the parent
generation: a `gfbf-2023b` dependency in a source recipe becomes a
`gfbf-2024a` solver requirement in this example. Implicit tuples stay implicit
when Resolvo selects a dependency within the target hierarchy. A locked or
preferred cross-generation pin is emitted as an explicit four-element
EasyBuild tuple so the generated recipe records the artifact identity that the
lock selected.

# Validate generated recipes

```bash
eb-stack recipe format /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a/easyconfigs/g/GROMACS/*.eb
eb-stack recipe lint /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a/easyconfigs/g/GROMACS/*.eb

eb-stack recipe check \
  --recipe /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a/easyconfigs/g/GROMACS/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2024a.eb \
  --easyconfigs tests/repro_fixtures/universe_foss_2024a \
  --easyconfigs /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a/easyconfigs
```

Resolve missing dependencies by adding a real package bundle or authored recipe.
Checksums are positional: all sources first, then patches. Fix recipe content;
never bypass the packaging gate.

# Solve the multi-root stack

Use `stack solve` when the campaign also needs a generation-wide lock, build
list, or baseline diff:

```bash
eb-stack stack solve \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \
  --stack-policy fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/policies/prefer_newer.json \
  --baseline-easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \
  --lock-out /tmp/annual-stack.lock.json \
  --sbom-out /tmp/annual-stack.cdx.json \
  --build-list-out /tmp/annual-build.list \
  --stack-diff-out /tmp/annual-stack.diff.md
```

The whole-stack policy and package stack-policy solve related but distinct
problems: JSON chooses a multi-root stack; TOML controls preferred/locked pins
and exclusions for one generated product profile.

# Validate target routing

```bash
podman build -t eb-stack-rocky9 \
  -f skills/new-package/container/rocky9/Containerfile \
  skills/new-package/container/rocky9

eb-stack target doctor \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9
```

The doctor must show healthy transport, executor, runtime, and EasyBuild
workload checks before a campaign claim is trusted.

# Drive every build campaign

```bash
eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9 \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a.campaign.json
```

Hermes owns the retry loop. OMP workers claim findings and repair according to
class:

| Class | Repair surface |
| --- | --- |
| transport / executor / runtime | target or site configuration |
| checksum | source digest and positional checksum list |
| patch | patch source or applicability |
| dependency-missing | manifest, profile, stack policy, or real dependency recipe |
| configure / compile / link | product configuration, toolchain, patch, or dependency selection |
| test / install / sanity | recipe build logic and verification |
| resource / timeout | scheduler sizing or retry policy |

Each resolution records action, evidence, and changed paths. Rerun the same
campaign state; successful stages supersede stale open findings.

# Report claims accurately

- **resolves** means every requested profile has a lock and recipe.
- **builds** means every emitted recipe succeeds through EasyBuild on the target.
- **binary-verified** means every declared verification command succeeds.

An annual bump is not complete while an affected campaign remains failed or a
required verification command is absent. The human operator owns branch/PR
publication; the campaign supplies the recipe set and evidence.

The executable procedure is `skills/annual-bump/SKILL.md`.

# Author a new package from conda-forge or Spack

This workflow turns a foreign package recipe into a canonical manifest,
planned Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), Resolvo profile locks, conventional EasyBuild recipes, and a
persisted build-evaluation campaign. It is the workflow used for conda-forge
eOn and Spack QMCPACK fixtures.

# Inputs

Collect these inputs:

1. a conda-forge `meta.yaml`/`recipe.yaml` or Spack `package.py`;
2. one or more public package-config TOML files;
3. an EasyBuild robot tree, with site overlays passed after upstream;
4. a stack-policy TOML file for preferred pins, locked pins, and exclusions.
5. positional SHA-256 values for source artifacts whose foreign metadata has
   only a version control system (VCS) commit or tag.

Package TOML carries explicit foreign-to-EasyBuild aliases, package/build
policy, and installable product choices. Each profile emits a separate `.eb`
file. Message Passing Interface (MPI) and OpenMP toolchain options alone do not create a suffix; an
independently loadable ABI or feature variant does. Parser code handles foreign
syntax, never package names.

# Inspect the foreign recipe

```bash
eb-stack package inspect \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \
  --format conda-forge \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \
  --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/eon-inspect
```

Inspect `package.plan.json` and `package.sbom.cdx.json`. The parser preserves
source spans, dependency roles, conda selectors, Spack `when=` conditions,
variants, conflicts, requirements, and static build flags. Dynamic foreign
logic becomes a residual rather than an invented fact.

Spack input is parsed as Python syntax but never imported or executed. Literal
collections and bounded loops are evaluated statically, so data-driven
`variant()` and `depends_on()` declarations behave like direct calls. A call
with a runtime value is omitted from solver input and reported with its source
location.

Inspection may report `source:missing-sha256` for a commit-pinned Spack
release. A VCS commit does not determine the byte hash of the generated source
archive. Pass the reviewed archive hash to `package plan` with one
`--source-checksum` per source artifact; the planner does not invent or omit
packaging checksums.

For QMCPACK:

```bash
eb-stack package inspect \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/spack_qmcpack/package.py \
  --format spack \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \
  --package-config examples/packages/qmcpack.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/qmcpack-inspect
```

# Define package policy and product profiles

A package layer can replace or extend parser-derived metadata without changing
the parser. `examples/packages/common.toml` provides cross-ecosystem aliases;
later layers may replace package metadata, build policy, aliases, virtuals,
solver exclusions, and profiles.

An alias maps a foreign dependency identity to an EasyBuild provider. Use the
short string form when both names use the same version domain:

```toml
[dependencies.aliases]
libcurl = "cURL"
```

Use the structured form when the foreign dependency is a component supplied by
a larger EasyBuild package. `constraint = "drop"` prevents the component's
version from being interpreted as the provider's version:

```toml
[dependencies.aliases]
"py-setuptools" = { provider = "Python", constraint = "drop" }
```

The original foreign spelling and constraint remain in dependency provenance.
Aliases only control robot matching and solving; they do not teach the parser
about a package.

Easyblock-specific parameters are typed TOML data. They are emitted as normal
Python values, but configuration cannot inject Python expressions:

```toml
[build.easyconfig_parameters]
general_packages = ["ASPHERE", "KSPACE", "MOLECULE"]
build_shared_libs = true

[[profiles]]
name = "cuda"

[profiles.easyconfig_parameters]
cuda_compute_capabilities = ["80", "90"]
```

Build-level values apply to every product profile. A profile value with the
same key replaces the build-level value for that emitted recipe.

Use a requirement when EasyBuild product policy needs a dependency that the
foreign recipe does not declare. If a matching foreign edge exists, the
requirement makes that edge unconditional and merges its roles. Otherwise it
creates a canonical dependency before the SBOM and Resolvo lock are produced:

```toml
[[dependencies.requirements]]
name = "CMake"
constraint = ">=3.30"
roles = ["build"]

[[dependencies.requirements]]
name = "VTK"
roles = ["run"]
```

Do not put selected versions in this table merely to reproduce a neighboring
easyconfig. Constraints describe package compatibility; stack preferences and
distribution pins belong in Resolvo policy.

Patches are artifacts, not bare recipe text. Every patch has a filename and a
reviewed SHA-256. EasyBuild checksum order is all sources followed by all
patches:

```toml
[build]
patches_mode = "merge"

[[build.patches]]
filename = "Orbit-2.0-portability.patch"
sha256 = "4f43b42fdcf84d0cf634d993dd944f252c8243dc612a919fe2825d56f937c8eb"
source = "patches/Orbit-2.0-portability.patch"
```

A layer that declares `build.patches` replaces the preceding list unless it
sets `patches_mode = "merge"`. Merge mode preserves foreign recipe patches,
adds new filenames, and replaces an existing artifact when the layer supplies
the same filename. This lets reviewed EasyBuild metadata refine a foreign
patch without duplicating it.

`package inspect` records a blocking `patch:missing-sha256` residual for an
unchecked patch. `package plan` refuses to emit a buildable bundle until every
source and patch checksum is present. Relative patch sources resolve against
the package TOML file, and `package plan` copies verified patch bytes beside
the emitted easyconfig.

A QMCPACK profile set commonly contains a default MPI+OpenMP build and a
separate `-complex` recipe:

```toml
schema_version = 1

[package]
name = "QMCPACK"

[[profiles]]
name = "default"
default = true
platform = "linux"
architecture = "x86_64"
versionsuffix = []
config_options = ["-DQMC_MPI=ON", "-DQMC_OMP=ON", "-DQMC_COMPLEX=OFF"]

[profiles.toolchain_options]
usempi = true
openmp = true

[[profiles.verification_commands]]
program = "bash"
args = ["-lc", "module load {module} && qmcpack --version"]

[[profiles]]
name = "complex"
default = false
versionsuffix = ["-complex"]
config_options = ["-DQMC_MPI=ON", "-DQMC_OMP=ON", "-DQMC_COMPLEX=ON"]
```

`platform` and `architecture` are target context for foreign selectors. Put a
site-wide value such as `platform = "linux"` in a common package layer, then
override it in a product profile only when that output targets a different
environment. Resolvo sees dependencies only after selectors are materialized
against this explicit context.

Verification placeholders are `{module}`, `{package}`, `{version}`,
`{profile}`, and `{versionsuffix}`.

# Put stack knowledge inside Resolvo

Site or distribution pins are solver input, not a text rewrite after solving:

```toml
schema_version = 1
name = "foss-2026.1"
toolchain = { name = "foss", version = "2026.1" }

[[pins]]
name = "HDF5"
version_requirement = "==2.1.1"
mode = "preferred"
source = "site stack"

[[pins]]
name = "PyTorch"
version_requirement = "==2.9.1"
toolchain = { name = "foss", version = "2024a" }
versionsuffix = ""
mode = "preferred"
source = "distribution stack"
```

A preferred pin is favored when jointly feasible. Resolvo may choose another
compatible candidate and records the requested version, toolchain,
versionsuffix, selected identity, and fallback. A locked pin cannot fall back.
Omitting `toolchain` leaves the pin unconstrained within the target hierarchy;
cross-generation admission requires an explicit toolchain. Omitting
`versionsuffix` leaves that part of the artifact identity unconstrained.
Candidate exclusions record known target/build evidence and stay visible in
the profile lock.

# Plan the complete bundle

`scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh` creates a checkout of the pinned easybuilders
trees and writes `env.sh`. Source it so `EB_EASYCONFIGS` is the
`easybuild/easyconfigs` directory of easybuild-easyconfigs develop.

```bash
scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh
set -a
source "${EB_UPSTREAM_CACHE:-$HOME/.cache/eb-stack/upstream}/env.sh"
set +a
mkdir -p /tmp/eb-stack/robot /tmp/eb-stack/overlay /tmp/eb-stack/bundles
rsync -a "$EB_EASYCONFIGS"/ /tmp/eb-stack/robot/
rsync -a fixtures/eon_core_rgpot/easyconfigs/ /tmp/eb-stack/overlay/

eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \
  --format conda-forge \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \
  --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \
  --easyconfigs "$EB_EASYCONFIGS" \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/eon_core_rgpot/easyconfigs \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/eon-foss-2026.1.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon
```

Against easybuild-easyconfigs develop `981d2123dd` that prints:

```
closure_plan=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/closure.plan.json
closure_sbom=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/closure.sbom.cdx.json
build_order=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/build-order.json
manifest=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/package.plan.json
sbom=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/package.sbom.cdx.json
lock=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/locks/default.lock.json
easyconfig=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0-foss-2026.1.eb
patch=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0_safemath-eigen5-core-guard.patch
```

The command must produce a manifest, SBOM, one lock per requested profile,
one recipe per profile, and, because `--easyconfigs` is a discovery root,
`closure.plan.json`, `closure.sbom.cdx.json`, and `build-order.json`.
Run `recipe format`, `recipe lint`, and `recipe check`
against the upstream tree plus the bundle overlay.

```bash
eb-stack recipe format /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/*.eb
eb-stack recipe lint /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/*.eb
eb-stack recipe check \
  --recipe /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0-foss-2026.1.eb \
  --easyconfigs "$EB_EASYCONFIGS" \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/eon_core_rgpot/easyconfigs \
  --easyconfigs /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs
```

`recipe format` prints `rewritten`0 remaining`0`. `recipe lint` reports
`clean: true` with one maintainer warning, `EB_MAINT_TESTS_OFF`.
`recipe check` ends with `recipe resolves`. The locked build tools on
this tree are `CMake-4.2.1` and `pkgconf-2.5.1`, both `GCCcore-15.2.0`.

Missing robot dependencies are real package work. Close them with ordered
source roots and optional catalog overrides rather than inventing placeholders
or dummy checksums.

# Source-root discovery (package-neutral)

Configure local indexes so a package closure can resolve robot holes without a
committed per-package catalog entry:

```bash
eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \
  --format conda-forge \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \
  --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \
  --easyconfigs "$EB_EASYCONFIGS" \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/eon_core_rgpot/easyconfigs \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/eon-foss-2026.1.toml \
  --package-sources examples/package-sources/eon-companions.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-sources
```

Or pass roots directly with `--easybuild-source`, `--conda-source`,
`--spack-source`, and `--cargo-source` (repeatable; order is discovery order).

Resolution for each hole is robot-first, then:

1. optional catalog override for that identity;
2. EasyBuild recipes under easybuild source roots (annual-bump pipeline; source
   toolchain family is preserved: a `GCCcore` recipe retargets to the
   `GCCcore` member of the target hierarchy, not the composite parent);
3. exactly one compatible conda-forge or Spack recipe under foreign roots.

Ambiguous or incompatible providers fail with typed errors and candidate
evidence. Catalog entries remain optional ordered overrides.

# Catalog-backed robot holes

Pass one or more `--package-catalog` layers when `package plan` must recursively
close robot holes with explicit authoring inputs. Compatible robot candidates
still win; the catalog is only consulted for unsatisfied direct dependencies
before source-root discovery.

```bash
eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \
  --format conda-forge \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \
  --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \
  --easyconfigs "$EB_EASYCONFIGS" \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/eon_core_rgpot/easyconfigs \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/eon-foss-2026.1.toml \
  --package-catalog examples/package-catalog/eon.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-catalog
```

Each catalog entry maps an EasyBuild provider identity to authoring inputs.
Provider kinds:

| TOML `provider` | When to use |
| --- | --- |
| `foreign` (default; may be omitted) | The dependency has no EasyBuild recipe; plan from its conda-forge or Spack recipe, package-config layers, checksums, and product profile. |
| `easybuild-bump` | A compatible EasyBuild recipe already exists at another generation. Retarget it through the annual-bump pipeline (EasyBuild-origin plan, CycloneDX SBOM, Resolvo lock, deterministic emission). Do not replace that recipe with a foreign archive of a different artifact identity. |

`easybuild-bump` fields: `source` is the existing `.eb`, `toolchain` is the
target generation, optional `version` is the emitted package version used for
provider matching, and at most one `source_checksums` entry has annual-bump
semantics. Foreign-only fields (`format`, `package_config`, non-default
`profile`, multiple checksums) are typed catalog errors.

Companions are written under `packages/<name>-<version>-<toolchain>/`, share one
`easyconfigs/` overlay with the root, appear in topological `build-order.json`,
and contribute to `closure.sbom.cdx.json`. A bumped companion whose own
dependency is another catalog hole builds after that child and before its
consumer. See `examples/package-catalog/eon.toml`.

# Route the build

Keep reusable topology in a public base file and site details in a later layer:

```bash
podman build -t eb-stack-rocky9 \
  -f skills/new-package/container/rocky9/Containerfile \
  skills/new-package/container/rocky9

eb-stack target list \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml

eb-stack target doctor \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9
```

The selected target decides transport, executor, runtime, and EasyBuild
workload. A control host can therefore stage over SSH, submit through Slurm,
run on the host or in Podman/Docker, and invoke the site's EasyBuild command.
Use a runtime-specific `EASYBUILD_INSTALLPATH`, `work_root`, and `tmp_root` so
host-linked modules cannot leak into a container build. A shared
`EASYBUILD_SOURCEPATH` is safe for source archives.

# Run the Hermes/OMP repair loop

```bash
eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9 \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon.campaign.json
```

Hermes owns the campaign loop. OMP workers claim typed findings, repair the
manifest/profile/recipe/target layer appropriate to the class, record evidence,
and rerun the campaign. Build compatibility claims are not proof: configure,
compile, link, test, install, and sanity failures stay empirical findings until
the target build succeeds.

The endpoint is three separate claims:

- **resolves**: all profile locks and recipes exist;
- **builds**: every recipe succeeds through EasyBuild on the selected target;
- **binary-verified**: every declared verification command succeeds.

Follow `skills/new-package/SKILL.md` for the exact campaign procedure and
human-owned PR handoff.

# Site Python extras on EESSI

Turn a PyPI package or `requirements.txt` into an easyconfig that installs
on top of an EasyBuild robot. Inspect records `easyblock = PythonBundle`,
because ingest does not yet know whether the package brings extensions.
A plan of one package emits `PythonPackage` with its own sources and does
not write `exts_list`. Requirements the robot already provides become
dependencies on the providing bundle (`soupsieve` via
`Python-bundle-PyPI`, `numpy` via `SciPy-bundle`). A plan that still has
leftovers emits a `PythonBundle` and keeps only those leftovers in
`exts_list`.

Do not `pip install --target` and prepend `PYTHONPATH`. That shadows
toolchain-built extensions and has no claim on the European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI) compat layer.

# Inputs

1. Warehouse-shaped JSON (`info` + `urls`) or a `requirements.txt`;
2. the EESSI robot tree (or a fixture that mirrors its provides);
3. a stack policy that **locks** `Python`, `SciPy-bundle`, and
   `Python-bundle-PyPI` to the versions in the robot.
   See `examples/stacks/eessi-python-extras.toml`.

Inspect does not need a robot. Plan does.

# Inspect

```bash
eb-stack package inspect \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/pypi_bs4/pypi.json \
  --format pypi \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --out-dir /tmp/bs4-inspect
```

`package.plan.json` has `origin ` pypi` and `easyblock ` PythonBundle`.
Optional extras (`extra ==`) become residuals and are not solved.

A `requirements.txt` is also accepted. The first spec is the root
package; later specs are additional run dependencies.

# Plan

Source `env.sh` from `scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh` first.
`EB_EASYCONFIGS` is the develop easyconfigs tree.

```bash
eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/pypi_bs4/pypi.json \
  --format pypi \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/foreign_ingest/pypi_bs4/robot \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/eessi-python-extras.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/bs4
```

The lock collapses `soupsieve` to `Python-bundle-PyPI`. The emitted
recipe is `PythonPackage`, depends on `Python 3.13.1` and
`Python-bundle-PyPI 2025.04`, and has no `exts_list`. The checksum is
the one in the fixture. The plan's `easyblock` stays `PythonBundle`;
that class is what a multi-package overlay emits. A `PythonBundle`
recipe is for a set installed together, not for a single package.

Against easybuild-easyconfigs develop `981d2123dd`, with `--easyconfigs "$EB_EASYCONFIGS"`
after sourcing `env.sh`, the same package is already
provided and the command does not emit a recipe. The manifest residual
is:

```
beautifulsoup4 4.12.3 is already provided by BeautifulSoup 4.14.3 (beautifulsoup4 4.14.3); do not emit a pip overlay
```

The evidence path is `b/BeautifulSoup/BeautifulSoup-4.14.3-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb`.
The extra-only `lxml` requirement stays a parse residual.

```bash
eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/pypi_numpy/numpy.json \
  --format pypi \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/foreign_ingest/pypi_numpy/robot \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/eessi-python-extras.toml \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/numpy
```

Asking for `numpy` against a robot that already provides it writes no
recipe. `package.plan.json` has an `already-provided` residual:
`numpy 2.5.2 is already provided by SciPy-bundle 2025.06 (numpy 2.3.1)`.
A recipe that depends on numpy lists `SciPy-bundle`, not a pip numpy.
If the robot has no `SciPy-bundle` / `PyTorch`, the plan refuses rather
than emitting a wheel overlay.

A leftover that is not in EasyBuild yet (`eon-akmc`) keeps unsatisfied
PyPI run dependencies in the same `exts_list`. numpy still maps to
`SciPy-bundle`. A maturin/PyO3 leftover such as `readcon` is closed from
a Cargo source root (`--cargo-source` / `kind = "cargo"`) into a
companion `PythonPackage` (implicit `Rust` / `maturin` / `binutils`)
instead of a pip extension. Pass the crate metadata next to the PyPI
plan; do not `pip install` the crate into the overlay.

Resolvo picks every robot-provided name. Extra site packages that Warehouse
omits (measured `PyYAML` for `import eon`) go in the ingest as a second
Warehouse object in a JSON array, or as a later `requirements.txt` line.
A registry name (`--source eon-akmc`) fetches Warehouse once and writes
`ingest/pypi/<name>-<version>.json`. Replan from that dump; the Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solve does not
hit the network. Meson wrap natives come from `subprojects/*.wrap` in
the sdist tree next to the dump (or from `build_system.requires`). Do not
edit the emitted `.eb` to add those names: put the modules in
`--easyconfigs` and let the lock select them. An undeclared `import` is
a residual, not a silent SAT edge. A PEP 518 `build_system`
block with `build-backend = mesonpy` adds the listed build requirements
and emits `wrap_mode=default` plus the same cargo-on-EESSI isolation
prelude used by Cargo leftovers: drop host rustc wrappers, set
`LINKER=${CC:-gcc}`, put the EESSI compat `ld` on `PATH`, and point
`RUSTFLAGS -B` at that `ld`. The cargo target triple and compat arch
come from the build host (`rustc -vV`, `uname -m`), not from a
plan-time x86_64 literal. Hatchling and `meson-python` already on
`Python-bundle-PyPI` stay modules; they are not pip extras.

# Dependencies that state no version

A Python project routinely requires another package with no version. An
`exts_list` entry still needs one, so planning stops and asks for an index.
On this side the index is a pinned requirements file, matching what
`pip freeze` writes:

```bash
pip freeze > constraints.txt
eb-stack package plan ... --package-index constraints.txt
```

One `name==version` per line; comments and blank lines are ignored, and a line
that names a range rather than a version supplies nothing, since a range is not
a version. The same flag takes a Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) `PACKAGES` file for the R side; the
format is detected from the content.

# Install with the local target

Plan on the host. Install through `campaign run`:

```bash
scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh
set -a
source "${EB_UPSTREAM_CACHE:-$HOME/.cache/eb-stack/upstream}/env.sh"
set +a
mkdir -p /tmp/eb-stack/robot /tmp/eb-stack/bundles
rsync -a "$EB_EASYCONFIGS"/ \
  /tmp/eb-stack/robot/

podman build -t eb-stack-rocky9 \
  -f skills/new-package/container/rocky9/Containerfile \
  skills/new-package/container/rocky9

eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/bs4 \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9 \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/bs4.campaign.json
```

`examples/targets/eessi-extend.toml` is the target whose runtime command
is `eessi_container.sh`. The local target above is the one this checkout
runs. `scripts/eessi-extend-eb.sh` is the wrapper that target execs.

User one-offs stay as `python -m venv --system-site-packages` on EESSI
Python. This workflow is for a shared site or project extra.

# Site R extras on EESSI

Turn a Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) DESCRIPTION, CRAN JSON object, or package list into a
`Bundle` easyconfig with `exts_defaultclass = 'RPackage'`. Base-R
packages (`methods`, `utils`, ...) are dropped. `R (>= x)` becomes a
dependency on the EasyBuild `R` module. Packages already listed in
`R-bundle-CRAN` `exts_list` are satisfied as provides.

# Inputs

1. a DESCRIPTION file, `cran.json`, or a one-spec-per-line package list;
2. the European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI) robot tree;
3. a stack policy that locks `R` and `R-bundle-CRAN` to the versions
   in the robot. See `examples/stacks/eessi-r-extras.toml`.

# Inspect

```bash
eb-stack package inspect \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/cran_jsonlite/DESCRIPTION \
  --format cran \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --out-dir /tmp/jsonlite-inspect
```

`package.plan.json` has `origin = cran`. A single package, such as
this DESCRIPTION, has `easyblock = RPackage`, and that field stays
`RPackage` after planning. The emitted recipe is a `Bundle` with
`exts_defaultclass = 'RPackage'` and the package in `exts_list`.
Base-R imports are residuals (`cran-base`). A DESCRIPTION with no
digest is a `checksum` residual.

# Plan

The fixture robot does not already provide jsonlite, so this command
emits the bundle. The checksum is the placeholder stored with the
fixture. Against easybuild-easyconfigs develop, source `env.sh` from
`scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh` and pass `--easyconfigs "$EB_EASYCONFIGS"`
with the archive digest of
`jsonlite_1.8.8.tar.gz`. That tree already provides the package, so
plan prints the closure and does not emit a recipe.

```bash
eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/cran_jsonlite/cran.json \
  --format cran \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/foreign_ingest/cran_jsonlite/robot \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/eessi-r-extras.toml \
  --source-checksum bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/jsonlite
```

The develop run's manifest residual is:

```
jsonlite 1.8.8 is already provided by R 4.6.1 (jsonlite 2.0.0); do not emit a pip overlay
```

The evidence path is `r/R/R-4.6.1-gfbf-2026.1.eb`. DESCRIPTION files
rarely carry a SHA-256. Pass `--source-checksum` for the tarball, or use
a JSON document that already includes one. Plan refuses to emit a
buildable bundle without it. When the robot does not already provide
the package, plan emits `easyblock = Bundle` with
`exts_defaultclass = RPackage`.

# Check the recipe

Plan on the host, then confirm the recipe resolves against the same robot:

```bash
eb-stack recipe check \
  --recipe /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/jsonlite/easyconfigs/j/jsonlite/jsonlite-1.8.8-foss-2026.1.eb \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/foreign_ingest/cran_jsonlite/robot \
  --easyconfigs /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/jsonlite/easyconfigs
```

The check prints `recipe resolves` and finds `R-4.4.2 (foss-2026.1)`.

Project one-offs can keep using `R_LIBS_USER` instead of a site bundle.

# Dependencies that state no version

A CRAN package routinely imports another by bare name, with no version at all.
Nothing is wrong with that, but an `exts_list` entry needs one
concrete version, so planning stops with

```
processx is not in the robot, and ">=0" names no version to install as an extension. Give the ecosystem index with --package-index, or pin the dependency
```

That is what this fixture prints:

```bash
eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/cran_unpinned/cran.json \
  --format cran \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/foreign_ingest/cran_bundle/robot \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/eessi-r-extras.toml \
  --source-checksum dddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddd \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/quartoish
```

Give it an index in the control-file shape CRAN publishes. Versions and
`MD5sum` values for the leftovers come from that file:

```bash
cat > /tmp/PACKAGES <<'EOF'
Package: processx
Version: 3.8.4
MD5sum: 1111111111111111111111111111abcd

Package: rmarkdown
Version: 2.27
MD5sum: 2222222222222222222222222222abcd
EOF

eb-stack package plan \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/cran_unpinned/cran.json \
  --format cran \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/foreign_ingest/cran_bundle/robot \
  --stack-policy examples/stacks/eessi-r-extras.toml \
  --package-index /tmp/PACKAGES \
  --source-checksum dddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddd \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/quartoish
```

The index is a control file: stanzas of `Field: value` separated by blank
lines. Versions for unpinned leftovers come from it, and so do their checksums,
since CRAN publishes an `MD5sum` per package and EasyBuild accepts a tagged
`md5:` value. It is a file, so a plan stays reproducible
and works offline against a copy taken at a known time.

Without an index the error above is the right outcome: installing whatever
version happens to be current, unrecorded, is worse than stopping.

# When this emits a Bundle

Inspect records `RPackage`. Plan emits a `Bundle` with
`exts_defaultclass = 'RPackage'` and the package, or its leftovers, in
`exts_list`. A single package whose imports the robot already carries
still uses that shape, because a lone `RPackage` recipe has nowhere to
put a later leftover:

```python
easyblock = 'Bundle'
exts_defaultclass = 'RPackage'
exts_list = [
    ('jsonlite', '1.8.8', {...}),
]
```

`plan_cran_emits_a_single_r_package` is jsonlite alone.
`plan_cran_with_leftovers_emits_an_r_bundle` puts `processx` and
`rmarkdown` in the same list. The index plan above writes
`('processx', '3.8.4'` and the `md5:` value from the index.

An already-provided import collapses to its provider instead of becoming an
extension, through the same mechanism Python packages use: an `R-bundle-CRAN`
in the robot tree satisfies a requirement for one of its `exts_list` entries.

# eOn on EESSI with EESSI-extend and eb --robot

Install eOn, and the dependencies the European Environment for Scientific
Software Installations (EESSI) lacks, into a user or project prefix on top of
EESSI. EasyBuild's robot resolves the chain. Then build
eOn from a working tree against the same modules for development.

The build ran on 2026-09-21 and the development build on 2026-09-25, both
against EESSI 2026.06 on an AMD Zen 5 (`x86_64/amd/zen5`) Slurm node with
EasyBuild 5.4.0 from EESSI. The robot dry run was repeated on 2026-09-25 on an
Intel laptop (`x86_64/intel/haswell`). The easyconfigs come from the open
easyconfigs pull request #26480 (eOn 2.17.10 on `foss/2026.1`). Until that pull
request is merged, `--from-pr 26480` is how they reach the robot.

# What EESSI provides and what gets built

EESSI 2026.06 provides `foss/2026.1` (GCC 15.2.0, OpenMPI, FlexiBLAS, FFTW), Meson,
Ninja, CMake, Eigen, Rust and Python. The robot builds the rest, eleven
easyconfigs at `GCCcore-15.2.0` plus eOn. A dry run (`eb -D` with the command
below) reports 88 modules already present and these 12 to build:

| Module | Why EESSI lacks it |
| --- | --- |
| `Highway/1.4.0`, `inih/62`, `fmt/12.2.0`, `Catch2/3.14.0` | not in the 2026.06 stack |
| `cargo-c/0.10.23` | build dependency of `readcon-core` |
| `robin-map/1.4.1`, `nanobind/2.13.0` | `nanobind` needs `robin-map` |
| `CapnProto/1.4.0`, `quill/11.1.0`, `readcon-core/0.13.1`, `rgpot/3.0.0` | new in pull request #26480 |
| `eOn/2.17.10-foss-2026.1` | new in pull request #26480 |

The first full run built the chain in 13 minutes 38 seconds on 32 cores. With
the dependencies installed, a rebuild of eOn alone takes about 2.5 minutes.

# Prerequisites

1. EESSI mounted at `/cvmfs/software.eessi.io` through the CernVM File System (CVMFS).
   See [[*Without root][Without root]] when no
   administrator can install the CVMFS client.
2. A prefix for the installs. It must exist before `EESSI-extend` loads, or
   the module refuses to load:

```bash
   export EESSI_USER_INSTALL=$HOME/EESSI      # or EESSI_PROJECT_INSTALL=/project/...
   mkdir -p "$EESSI_USER_INSTALL"
```

3. Optionally, a shallow clone of the easyconfigs `develop` branch as an extra
   robot path, for recipes newer than the EasyBuild release in EESSI:

```bash
   scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh
   set -a
   source "${EB_UPSTREAM_CACHE:-$HOME/.cache/eb-stack/upstream}/env.sh"
   set +a
   # "$EB_EASYCONFIGS_DEVELOP" is the pinned easyconfigs checkout
```

# Build eOn with the robot

`scripts/eessi-extend-eb.sh` sources EESSI's init, loads `EESSI-extend`,
isolates Cargo from host wrappers, and execs `eb`. On this checkout the
build runs through the local Podman target, which invokes `eb --robot`
on the planned eOn bundle. The bundle path has to sit under
`/tmp/eb-stack`, because that is the directory the target mounts.

```bash
podman build -t eb-stack-rocky9 \
  -f skills/new-package/container/rocky9/Containerfile \
  skills/new-package/container/rocky9

eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-tutorial \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9 \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-tutorial.campaign.json
```

Plan that bundle with the commands in [the tutorial](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../tutorial.html.md)
before this run. `campaign run` stays in the foreground and starts
`eb --robot` inside the image.

What each option is for:

- `--from-pr 26480` puts the pull request's easyconfigs first on the robot
  path. Drop it once the recipes are in an EasyBuild release.
- `--robot-paths=<develop tree>:` with the trailing colon appends the default
  robot path, so EESSI's own easyconfigs still resolve. `-r` turns the robot on.
- `--umask=022` matters for user installs: `EESSI-extend` sets umask 077 and the
  sticky bit when `EESSI_USER_INSTALL` is set. That is fine for a private
  prefix, but see [[*Without root][Without root]] for the case where it breaks module loads.
- `--dump-test-report` writes the report EasyBuild would post to the pull request.

The test report's summary on success:

```
Build succeeded for 1 out of 1 (total: 2 mins 27 secs)
 * SUCCESS eOn-2.17.10-foss-2026.1.eb
```

# Use the installed eOn

Read the campaign while it runs, from another shell:

```bash
eb-stack campaign status --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-tutorial.campaign.json
```

The modules land under
`$EESSI_USER_INSTALL/versions/2026.06/software/linux/$EESSI_SOFTWARE_SUBDIR/modules/all`,
so a second CPU target gets its own tree, and each host loads the build for
its own architecture.

# Develop eOn from a working tree

The installed modules are a development environment as well. eOn builds with
Meson, and its `develop` branch needs Meson 1.8 or newer, rgpot 3.2 or newer and
readcon-core 0.14.9 or newer. That is newer than the rgpot 3.0.0 and
readcon-core 0.13.1 in pull request #26480, so Meson takes those two from its
wraps (the compute node needs network for that) and everything else comes from
EESSI and the prefix.

This ran on 2026-09-25 as a 16-core Slurm job on EESSI 2026.06, with `develop`
at `1916f9a9`: `meson test --suite eon` reported 43 passed and 0 failed.
The build directory was outside `$HOME`, `CC`, `CXX`, and `FC` named the
EESSI compilers, and `CARGO_HOME` was a fresh directory. Iterate with
`meson compile -C $WORK/build` after each edit. Nothing here
installs into the EESSI prefix, so the code under development lives in the
working tree alone. `module use` on the prefix does what ~module load
EESSI-extend` does for `MODULEPATH~, without the EasyBuild settings that module
also sets.

Three host settings broke earlier attempts, each with its own error:

| Error | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mesonbuild'` | the compat layer's `usr/bin` was prepended to `PATH`; its `python3` ignores `EBPYTHONPREFIXES`, so Meson's shebang found a Python without Meson | leave the compat layer off the front of `PATH`; EESSI's GCC finds its linker without it |
| `gcc: error: unrecognized command-line option '-fuse-ld=/usr/bin/mold'` | Cargo reads `.cargo/config.toml` from every parent of its working directory, so a build under `$HOME` picked up the host's linker settings | build outside `$HOME` and set `CARGO_HOME` to a fresh directory |
| compilers run through the host's `sccache` | Meson wraps `cc` in a ccache it finds on `PATH` | name the compilers in `CC`, `CXX` and `FC` |

On EESSI 2025.06, the one Meson 1.8 module sits at `GCCcore-14.3.0`, which means
`foss/2025b` rather than `foss/2025a`.

# Without root

Where no administrator installs the CVMFS client, an unprivileged user runs
`cvmfs2` against a private cache with `-o libfuse=2`, then bind-mounts that
directory at the canonical path inside a user namespace. This checkout has
`/dev/fuse` and no `cvmfs2` package in its apt repositories, so the build
above uses the local Podman target instead of that mount.

The libfuse 2 path matters on some hosts: CVMFS 2.13.3's libfuse 3 path served
directory listings but never answered a file read against fuse3 3.18.2, while
the libfuse 2 path answered at once. Inside the namespace the process is uid 0,
which has four consequences for EasyBuild:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EasyBuild refuses to start | it will not run as root | `--allow-use-as-root-and-accept-consequences`; files still belong to the real user |
| sanity check: fake module unknown | Lmod as uid 0 skips a module directory without read and search for others; EESSI-extend's umask 077 makes it 0700 | `--umask=022` |
| tar: `Cannot change ownership to uid 1000` | the namespace maps uid 0 alone, so restoring archive owners fails (`cargo-c`, `CapnProto`) | `export TAR_OPTIONS=--no-same-owner` |
| every run rebuilds everything | a prefix first created under umask 077 hides all later modules from Lmod | once, as the real user: `find $EESSI_USER_INSTALL -type d ! -perm -o=rx -exec chmod o+rx {} +` |

A cancelled `eb` run also leaves its lock under `software/.locks/` in the prefix;
remove it before the next run.

# After pull request #26480 is merged

EESSI's software-layer easystacks pin recipes that are not in an EasyBuild
release with `from-commit` and a comment naming the pull request. The entries for
`easystacks/software.eessi.io/2026.06/eessi-2026.06-eb-5.4.0-2026.1.yml`:

```yaml
  - Highway-1.4.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb
  - inih-62-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb
  - fmt-12.2.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb
  - cargo-c-0.10.23-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb
  - Catch2-3.14.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb
  - robin-map-1.4.1-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb
  - nanobind-2.13.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb
  - eOn-2.17.10-foss-2026.1.eb:
      options:
        # see https://github.com/easybuilders/easybuild-easyconfigs/pull/26480
        from-commit: <merge commit of #26480>
```

The four other new recipes (`CapnProto`, `quill`, `readcon-core`, `rgpot`) carry
the same `from-commit` block. The EESSI build bot then builds the easystack for
each CPU target, and the prefix install above is no longer needed.

# Related

- [Site Python extras on EESSI](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/pypi-extend.html.md) and [site R extras](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/cran-extend.html.md) use
  the same `eessi-extend` target through `campaign run`.

# Spack on EESSI with EESSI installs as externals

Concretize a Spack package on top of installs that already have an
easyconfig beside them. Everything the prefix already has comes in as a
Spack external, and Spack builds the rest. The compiler is that prefix's
GCCcore, and the CPU target is `spack arch -t` on the machine running the
command.

The prefix in this checkout is CMake 3.31.3 on GCCcore 13.3.0. The Spack
checkout is the `eessi` branch of
[lorisercole/spack](https://github.com/lorisercole/spack), and EasyBuild
5.4.0 is installed in a venv so the script can parse the easyconfigs.

# What the script does

`scripts/eessi-spack-externals.py` reads the easyconfig that every install in the European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI)
keeps under `<install>/easybuild/`, walks the runtime dependency closure of the
modules you name, and writes a Spack `packages.yaml`:

- GCCcore becomes the `gcc` external with its compiler paths, and a
  `require: '@<version>'` so Spack compiles with it.
- Toolchains such as `foss`, `gompi` and `GCC` are skipped. Bundles are not
  registered themselves; their Python extensions become `py-*` externals, and
  a dependency on a bundle becomes a dependency on those.
- With `--spack-packages` (the output of `spack list`), names Spack does not
  package are left out and reported on stderr.

Compat-layer packages such as zlib, bzip2, ncurses and openssl are not in EESSI's
software layer, so they come from `spack external find` in step 4.

# Steps

The prefix in this repository is `tests/eessi_spack_fixtures`. It has
GCCcore 13.3.0 and CMake 3.31.3 built with that GCCcore. The script
records compiler paths `bin/gcc`, `bin/g++`, and `bin/gfortran` under
`tests/eessi_spack_fixtures/software/GCCcore/13.3.0`.

1. A Python that imports EasyBuild, and Spack. On Debian the `venv` module
   is the `python3-venv` package.
```bash
   sudo apt-get install -y python3-venv gfortran
   python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/easybuild
   ~/.venvs/easybuild/bin/pip install easybuild==5.4.0
   git clone --depth 1 --branch eessi https://github.com/lorisercole/spack.git /tmp/spack
   . /tmp/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh
```
2. Give Spack its own user scope. Do not set `SPACK_DISABLE_LOCAL_CONFIG`: it
   also drops the user scope, and Spack then never reads the generated file.
```bash
   export SPACK_USER_CONFIG_PATH=/tmp/spack-cfg SPACK_USER_CACHE_PATH=/tmp/spack-cache
   mkdir -p $SPACK_USER_CONFIG_PATH
```
3. Generate the externals for the modules the build should reuse.
   The script writes `packages.yaml` on stdout and names missing
   dependencies on stderr. For this fixture the stderr line is
   `not in the software layer: CMake/3.31.3-GCCcore-13.3.0 -> ncurses 6.5`.
```bash
   ~/.venvs/easybuild/bin/python scripts/eessi-spack-externals.py \
     --software tests/eessi_spack_fixtures \
     --target "$(spack arch -t)" \
     --spack-packages tests/eessi_spack_fixtures/spack-packages.txt \
     CMake/3.31.3-GCCcore-13.3.0 \
     > $SPACK_USER_CONFIG_PATH/packages.yaml
```
   The gcc entry has `require: '@13.3.0'` and `languages:='c,c++,fortran'`.
   The cmake entry depends on `gcc@13.3.0`.
4. Concretize. Both nodes are externals.
```bash
   spack spec -I cmake
```

# What to check in the spec

On this machine `spack arch -t` prints `icelake`, and the spec is:

```
[e]  cmake@3.31.3~doc+ncurses+ownlibs~qtgui build_system=generic build_type=Release platform=linux os=ubuntu24.04 target=icelake %c,cxx=gcc@13.3.0
[e]      ^gcc@13.3.0+binutils+bootstrap+futex~graphite+libsanitizer~mold~nvptx~piclibs~profiled~strip build_system=autotools build_type=Release languages:='c,c++,fortran' platform=linux os=ubuntu24.04 target=icelake
```

| Check | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| compiler on the root | `%c,cxx=gcc@13.3.0` |
| target on the root | the value of `spack arch -t` |
| `[e]` nodes | `cmake@3.31.3` and `gcc@13.3.0` |

A root on a different gcc version means Spack did not read the generated
file: check `SPACK_USER_CONFIG_PATH`. An error that an external "there is
no such external spec" names a dependency the script did not emit; rerun
step 3 with `--spack-packages`.

# Repair a failed campaign

Use this procedure when `eb-stack campaign run` records a failed attempt. The
campaign state already contains the routed command, compact nested log, error
class, repair disposition, and ownership queue. Keep that evidence attached to
the same state file through every retry.

# Inspect the active finding

Start with a compact view, then read the complete finding before changing a
recipe or target:

The bundle is the one [Author a new package](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/new-package.html.md) writes at
`/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon`. The target below names an EasyBuild program
that is not on `PATH`, so the attempt fails at once and the finding id
is `attempt:1:finding:1`.

```bash
eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon \
  --config examples/targets/missing-easybuild.toml \
  --target missing-eb \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-repair.campaign.json

eb-stack campaign status --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-repair.campaign.json |
  jq '{status, attempts, claims, current_recipe,
       active_findings: [.findings[] |
         select(.status == "open" or .status == "in-progress") |
         {id, class, disposition, stage, recipe, summary, owner,
          command, exit_code, evidence}]}'
```

`campaign run` exits 1 and prints `campaign build failed with typed findings`.
The status document has `status ` failed`, `resolves ` true`, `builds = false`,
and one open finding of class `runtime`. The evidence names
`/definitely/missing/eb-stack-easybuild`.

The three claims are independent. A failed build can retain `resolves: true`
while `builds` and `binary_verified` remain false. Resolving a finding records
a repair decision; only a successful campaign retry establishes a build claim.

# Check the routing layers

Run the target doctor for `transport`, `executor`, or `runtime` findings, and
before diagnosing a product failure on a target whose configuration changed:

```bash
eb-stack target doctor \
  --config examples/targets/missing-easybuild.toml \
  --target missing-eb
```

Doctor exits 1. stderr is:

```
error: target missing-eb doctor failed
```

Stdout is the check JSON. The easybuild check fails, and its `stderr`
field is:

```
"stderr": "spawn target command /definitely/missing/eb-stack-easybuild: No such file or directory (os error 2)"
```

It does not build the recipe. Compare that program with the failed
finding. A healthy local target is:

```bash
eb-stack target doctor \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9
```

Container build and install roots belong to one runtime ABI. Keep Cargo and
other package-manager build directories outside bind-mounted personal
configuration ancestry. The [target reference](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../reference/targets.html.md) includes a complete neutral
mount-alias pattern for sites whose durable storage lives below a home
directory.

# Claim the finding

Use a stable worker name. Claims prevent Hermes and OMP workers from applying
different repairs to the same evidence:

```bash
eb-stack campaign finding claim \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-repair.campaign.json \
  --id attempt:1:finding:1 \
  --owner hermes
```

The same owner may claim again safely. Another owner receives an ownership
error and must select a different open finding.

# Choose the repair surface

Treat the class as the first place to inspect, not as a substitute for the
compiler, linker, test, or runtime evidence.

| Finding class | First check | Typical changed artifact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `transport` | Host reachability and staged paths | Private site target layer |
| `executor` | Scheduler command and allocation | Private site target layer |
| `runtime` | Runtime executable, image, mounts, ABI, environment | Target TOML or container definition |
| `interrupted` | Absence of the prior routed workload and ownership of the campaign lock | No artifact for a clean retry; target repair when a workload survived |
| `source` | Upstream URL, mirror, cache, and target-runtime reachability | Recipe source or target runtime |
| `checksum` | Source/patch order and upstream digest | Easyconfig checksum list |
| `patch` | Patch source, order, and applicability | Patch plus Easyconfig |
| `dependency-missing` | Manifest/profile requirement and robot candidates | Profile, stack policy, or dependency recipe |
| `configure` | Product options and detected dependencies | Easyconfig, profile, or patch |
| `compile` | First source-level diagnostic and effective flags | Easyconfig, patch, dependency, or target environment |
| `link` | ABI, selected libraries, and link interface | Easyconfig, patch, dependency, or target environment |
| `test` | Failing product assertion and runtime environment | Product repair or target environment |
| `install` | Install paths, permissions, and EasyBlock behavior | Easyconfig or target filesystem |
| `sanity` | Declared files, commands, and loaded module | Easyconfig or profile verification command |
| `resource` | Kernel/scheduler evidence and parallelism | Executor allocation or `EASYBUILD_PARALLEL` |
| `timeout` | Routed timeout and scheduler wall time | Executor or target policy |
| `unknown` | Exact command and nested log | Evidence-dependent |

A solver-compatible selection is not a promise that source code compiles. A
real compiler incompatibility remains a `compile` repair owned by the campaign
loop. Add a stack exclusion or change a pin only when the evidence identifies
the selected dependency identity as the cause.

For recipe changes, run the nearest mechanical checks before the campaign:

```bash
eb-stack recipe format /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/*.eb
eb-stack recipe lint /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/*.eb
eb-stack recipe check \
  --recipe /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0-foss-2026.1.eb \
  --easyconfigs /tmp/src/easybuild-easyconfigs/easybuild/easyconfigs \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/eon_core_rgpot/easyconfigs \
  --easyconfigs /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon/easyconfigs
```

Checksum lists are positional: every source first, then every patch. A missing
dependency hint is a repair queue, including candidates at other generations;
it is not permission to bypass recipe validation.

Build failures are not package parser policy. Classify with
`BuildFindingClass`, claim ownership, and record a `FindingResolution`
(action, evidence, changed paths). Do not invent package-specific parser
branches or arbitrary manifest mutation tools to clear a finding.

# Record the repair

Resolve the owned finding with an action, evidence from the nearest check, and
every changed artifact:

```bash
eb-stack campaign finding resolve \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-repair.campaign.json \
  --id attempt:1:finding:1 \
  --owner hermes \
  --action "point the EasyBuild command at the program the target image provides" \
  --evidence "target doctor easybuild check names the missing program" \
  --change examples/targets/local-podman.toml
```

The resolution is an audit record. The finding status becomes `resolved`
and the owner stays `hermes`.

# Retry the same state

Run the original bundle and target with the same state path:

```bash
eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9 \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon-repair.campaign.json
```

The command stays in the foreground. Run it under the site's terminal or
service supervisor and inspect status from another shell. A successful attempt
retains resolved findings and supersedes matching open findings, then advances
`builds` and `binary_verified` only when their commands succeed.

If the controller exits, its advisory state guard releases automatically.
Confirm that its container, scheduler job, or remote command is absent before
retrying because a routed workload can outlive the controller. Reuse the state
file so attempt history and evidence remain one coherent record.

# Solve a consistent stack lock

Use `stack solve` for a multi-root EasyBuild generation lock. This is separate
from per-profile stack-policy TOML used by `package plan` and `package bump`.

# Write a whole-stack policy

```json
{
  "toolchain": {"name": "foss", "version": "2025b"},
  "roots": ["GROMACS"],
  "root_priority": ["GROMACS"],
  "pins": [],
  "forbid": [],
  "objective": "prefer_newer",
  "require_upgrade": {"name": "GROMACS", "relative_to_baseline": true}
}
```

Roots and all declared runtime/build requirements are co-selected. Explicit
`root_priority` makes multi-root optimization stable under root-list order.

# Solve with overlays and reports

```bash
eb-stack stack solve \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \
  --stack-policy fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/policies/prefer_newer.json \
  --baseline-easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \
  --lock-out /tmp/solve-lock.lock.json \
  --sbom-out /tmp/solve-lock.cdx.json \
  --build-list-out /tmp/solve-build.list \
  --stack-diff-out /tmp/solve-stack.diff.md
```

`--easyconfigs` is repeatable. Later paths override earlier paths for the same
name, version, toolchain, and versionsuffix identity. A site-only package is
added to the universe normally.

When the baseline tree includes several generations, use
`--baseline-toolchain-version` to select one explicitly. A relative
`require_upgrade` fails if the baseline package is absent or no newer candidate
is jointly feasible.

# Pin or forbid candidates

Policy pins use EasyBuild-shaped requirements such as `=`0.3.24`, `>`1.14`,
or a compound range. `forbid` accepts a package name or full easyconfig path.
An unsatisfiable solve reports package names and versions from the actual
candidate graph.

# Emit an SBOM from an existing lock

```bash
eb-stack stack sbom --lock /tmp/solve-lock.lock.json --out /tmp/solve-lock.cdx.json
```

`stack sbom`, the Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) command, reads runtime and build edges, checksums, and source URLs
back from the easyconfigs the lock names. A dependency counts only when
that name is also in the lock. A path that cannot be read contributes
nothing for that component. `--sbom-out` during `stack solve` writes the
same document while the candidate graph is still in memory.

# Order every pinned build

`stack solve` picks one version of each name. `stack order` keeps every
pinned build, and a name can stay twice. `stack order` writes the builds
in dependency order:

```bash
eb-stack stack order \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \
  --root GROMACS --root 'OpenBLAS==0.3.27' \
  --out /tmp/build-order.txt \
  --easystack-out /tmp/order.yml \
  --hashes-out /tmp/hashes.txt
```

`--oldest` selects the oldest admissible version of an unpinned
requirement. The hash file is one `<sha256>  <module>` line per build.
See [the CLI reference](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../reference/cli.html.md).

See [the policy reference](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../reference/policy.html.md) and
[the format reference](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../reference/formats.html.md).

# Emit a build list and stack diff

Goal: alongside the lock, get an install-ordered build list for a
build pipeline and a markdown diff you can paste straight into a pull
request. The commands below write those files under `/tmp`.

# Add the two flags to solve

`stack solve` accepts `--build-list-out` and `--stack-diff-out`. They are
independent: pass either, both, or neither.

```bash
eb-stack stack solve \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \
  --stack-policy fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/policies/prefer_newer.json \
  --baseline-easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \
  --lock-out /tmp/emit-stack.lock.json \
  --sbom-out /tmp/emit-stack.cdx.json \
  --build-list-out /tmp/emit-build.list \
  --stack-diff-out /tmp/emit-stack.diff.md
```

`--stack-diff-out` needs a baseline lock. Omit `--baseline-easyconfigs` and
the first `--easyconfigs` tree is that baseline. Pass `--baseline-easystack`
to diff against what those easystacks install. A caller that can form no
baseline fails and names `--baseline-easyconfigs` or `--baseline-easystack`.
There is no `--baseline` flag.

To diff against what a software layer already installs, pass its easystacks as
the baseline instead of an older tree:

```bash
eb-stack stack solve \
  --easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \
  --toolchain foss/2025b --root GROMACS \
  --baseline-easystack fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easystacks/gromacs-2024.4.yml \
  --build-list-out /tmp/site.list \
  --build-list-excludes-baseline \
  --stack-diff-out /tmp/easystack.diff.md \
  --lock-out /tmp/easystack.lock.json
```

The baseline label is the toolchain (`foss-2025b`), the same shape as the
solved lock. `/tmp/site.list` contains the version-bumped modules in build
order, and leaves out what the easystack already installs:

```text
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenBLAS-0.3.27-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenMPI-5.0.3-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b.eb
```

`/tmp/easystack.diff.md` opens with `Baseline (`foss-2025b`) to solved (`foss-2025b`)`.
Unchanged: 2 (FFTW, Python). Version-bumped: 3 (GROMACS 2024.4 to 2025.0,
OpenBLAS 0.3.24 to 0.3.27, OpenMPI 4.1.6 to 5.0.3).

# Read the build list

```text
cat /tmp/emit-build.list
```

One easyconfig path per line, dependencies before the packages that need
them (a topological sort over the co-selected stack, ties broken by package
name for a deterministic order):

```text
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/FFTW-3.3.10-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenBLAS-0.3.27-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenMPI-5.0.3-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/Python-3.12.3-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b.eb
```

Feed this straight into a sequential build pipeline: `xargs -n1 eb build`,
a Jenkins matrix step, or a plain shell loop.

# Read the stack diff

Every co-selected package is classified against the baseline lock as
`unchanged`, `added`, `removed`, or `version-bumped`:

```markdown
# Stack diff

Baseline (`foss-2025a`) to solved (`foss-2025b`).

## Summary

- **unchanged**: 2
- **added**: 0
- **removed**: 0
- **version-bumped**: 3

## Packages

### FFTW: unchanged

- Baseline: `3.3.10` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/FFTW-3.3.10-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `3.3.10` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/FFTW-3.3.10-foss-2025b.eb`)

### GROMACS: version-bumped

- Baseline: `2024.1` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/GROMACS-2024.1-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `2025.0` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b.eb`)
- Change: `2024.1` to `2025.0`

### OpenBLAS: version-bumped

- Baseline: `0.3.23` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/OpenBLAS-0.3.23-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `0.3.27` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenBLAS-0.3.27-foss-2025b.eb`)
- Change: `0.3.23` to `0.3.27`

### OpenMPI: version-bumped

- Baseline: `4.1.5` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/OpenMPI-4.1.5-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `5.0.3` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenMPI-5.0.3-foss-2025b.eb`)
- Change: `4.1.5` to `5.0.3`

### Python: unchanged

- Baseline: `3.12.3` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/Python-3.12.3-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `3.12.3` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/Python-3.12.3-foss-2025b.eb`)
```

A tree baseline and an easystack baseline are both labelled with the
toolchain (`foss-2025a`, `foss-2025b`). Paste the file
body directly into a pull request description; every line names a real
version and a real easyconfig path.

# Next steps

- [Format reference](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../reference/formats.html.md) for the exact build-list and
  stack-diff grammar, and the CycloneDX 1.5 Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) shape (`cyclonedx-bom`).
- [Solve a consistent stack lock](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/solve-lock.html.md) if you have not run
  `eb-stack stack solve` yet.

# Bump an existing EasyBuild recipe

A bump is a canonical EasyBuild-origin package bundle. It emits a planned
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), a Resolvo lock, and a rewritten recipe; it does not use a separate text
rewrite API.

# Retarget the toolchain generation

```bash
eb-stack package bump \
  --source tests/repro_fixtures/gromacs/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2023b.eb \
  --toolchain foss/2024a \
  --easyconfigs tests/repro_fixtures/universe_foss_2024a \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a
```

The solver materializes the source recipe as a default profile, derives the
target toolchain hierarchy from the robot tree, and asks Resolvo for a jointly
feasible dependency selection. Existing robot artifacts keep independent
build-tool scopes, matching EasyBuild's installed-module model.

The output is:

```text
/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a/
  package.plan.json
  package.sbom.cdx.json
  locks/default.lock.json
  easyconfigs/g/GROMACS/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2024a.eb
```

# Use site overlays and stack preferences

Pass robot paths from general to specific. An explicit override is a
locked solver input. This fixture's universe already selects Python
3.12.3, and `--dep` records that pin:

```bash
eb-stack package bump \
  --source tests/repro_fixtures/gromacs/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2023b.eb \
  --toolchain foss/2024a \
  --easyconfigs tests/repro_fixtures/universe_foss_2024a \
  --dep Python=3.12.3 \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-dep
```

Preferred distribution pins participate in the Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solve and may fall back.
Locked pins are exact constraints. Both outcomes are recorded in the profile
lock, so a site preference never becomes an invisible post-solve edit.
When a selected pin belongs to another toolchain generation, the emitted
dependency tuple includes that toolchain explicitly. Source dependencies that
already use an explicit toolchain preserve their family and retarget its
generation before solving.

# Change the application version

```bash
eb-stack package bump \
  --source tests/repro_fixtures/gromacs/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2023b.eb \
  --toolchain foss/2024a \
  --version 2024.5 \
  --easyconfigs tests/repro_fixtures/universe_foss_2024a \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024.5
```

The emitter updates the package version, target toolchain, selected dependency
versions, conventional filename, and source checksum entry. Patches remain
explicit review work. Omitting the new checksum clears the old digest to an
empty string and records a residual. The bump never invents a digest.

To fill the digest without a separate EasyBuild run, pass `--fetch-checksums`.
The bump resolves `sources` and `source_urls` at the new version, downloads
each entry from those URLs in order, and writes the first source's SHA-256 into
the recipe and the SBOM, matching what `eb --inject-checksums` does on the
EasyBuild host. A git checkout, a missing URL or a failed download stays empty
and is listed in `sources.fetch.json` and as a `source:fetch` residual:

```bash
eb-stack package bump \
  --source tests/repro_fixtures/gromacs/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2023b.eb \
  --toolchain foss/2024a \
  --version 2024.5 \
  --fetch-checksums \
  --easyconfigs tests/repro_fixtures/universe_foss_2024a \
  --out-dir /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-fetch
```

The download fills `gromacs-2024.5.tar.gz` in `checksums`. The digest
written for that tarball is
`fecf06b186cddb942cfb42ee8da5f3eb2b9993e6acc0a2f18d14ac0b014424f3`.

With the source downloaded, the bump also tries every patch the tree cannot
decide against it, as EasyBuild's patch step will. A patch that applies stays,
one the release already contains or whose files are gone leaves `patches` and
`checksums`, and one that conflicts stays as an `undecided` `patch-decision`
residual that names the failed hunks. Such a patch needs a version rebased on
the new release before the recipe builds.

# Check and build

```bash
RECIPE=/tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a/easyconfigs/g/GROMACS/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2024a.eb

eb-stack recipe format "$RECIPE"
eb-stack recipe lint "$RECIPE"
eb-stack recipe check \
  --recipe "$RECIPE" \
  --easyconfigs tests/repro_fixtures/universe_foss_2024a \
  --easyconfigs /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a/easyconfigs

mkdir -p /tmp/eb-stack/robot
rsync -a tests/repro_fixtures/universe_foss_2024a/ /tmp/eb-stack/robot/

podman build -t eb-stack-rocky9 \
  -f skills/new-package/container/rocky9/Containerfile \
  skills/new-package/container/rocky9

eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9 \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/gromacs-2024a.campaign.json
```

`package bump` can establish **resolves**. Only the campaign's EasyBuild run can
establish **builds**, and only declared verification commands can establish
**binary-verified**. Follow `skills/annual-bump/SKILL.md` for batch operation and
repair handling.

# Declare root priority for multi-root optimization

Goal: when a policy has more than one root and they disagree on a shared
dependency's version, control which root wins the newest-version tie-break
instead of leaving it to incidental list order.

# The conflict

Two application roots, one shared dependency, mutually exclusive
requirements on it:

```python
# GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b.eb (newest GROMACS)
dependencies = [
    ('OpenMPI', '==4.1.6'),
]

# LAMMPS-2024.08-foss-2025b.eb (newest LAMMPS)
dependencies = [
    ('OpenMPI', '>=5.0.3'),
]
```

Both roots cannot get their newest version at once: only one `OpenMPI`
version is co-selected per lock. Feasibility, checked by resolvo's conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) Boolean satisfiability (SAT) core, will
happily return **a** consistent assignment, but which one depends on solver
internals unless the policy says which root matters more. See
